en: The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Invincible Great Brightness King Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Great Teacher of the Dharma, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Fātian, at Nālandā Monastery in Magadha, Central India.
Translated by Imperial Decree. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra, Ānanda, and the others:
"I shall now proclaim the Vidyārājñī Dhāraṇī of Invincibility."
For the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to those humans and devas,
should there be vetālas, bhūtas, or others who,
regarding this Great Vidyārājñī, initiate fundamental karmic actions to create various obstacles and difficulties.
Even if yakṣas or rākṣasas should arise with violent and evil karma,
desiring to destroy this vidyārāja, they shall be unable to destroy it.
Then he spoke the mantra:
Tadyathā: hāsani, vihāsani, huru huru, svāhā. If there is a person of wisdom and intelligence...
For one who, with a mind free from doubt, respectfully upholds this heart-mantra of the Vidyārāja,
whether that person is at the gate of a king or amidst lions,
on a road or off a road, [no harm shall come].
One should constantly keep this in mind.
Even when encountering the abode of the Māra-king or meeting with those who are one's enemies,
this Vidyārāja will always provide protection, so that there shall be no fear whatsoever.
Then he spoke the mantra:
*tadyathā | dumi | dumi | dumavaṭe | svāhā*. If there should be a woman...
For one who single-mindedly upholds it,
and further writes it down and wears it upon their crown,
whatever wealth they possess—
May there be perpetual abundance without depletion,
and may all retinues attain peace and happiness.
Then he spoke this mantra:
Tadyathā: jva jva, jvani, svāhā. If there is a woman who is pregnant...
After a long time, they will no longer give rise to various sufferings and afflictions.
By upholding this vidyā-mantra, all shall attain easy rebirth.
Then he spoke the mantra:
Tadyathā: kaśa kaśa, vikaśa, mahākaśa, svāhā. If there should be anyone in the midst of an army array who is killing one another...
This invincible [mantra] shall provide protection so that all may dwell in peace.
He then spoke the mantra:
*Tadyathā | ṭaṭa ṭhu ṭha | ciṭhu | svāhā*. If there should be anyone who, at a time of delusion or intoxication...
Whether in sleep or dreams, or even while walking or standing,
that multitude of *bhūtas* will be unable to cause them any disturbance, and they shall always attain peace and happiness.
Furthermore, if there are people who, with a sincere heart, constantly uphold, recite, and proclaim this *Aparājita*, [they shall likewise be protected].
Providing protection throughout the day and night,
listen with single-minded devotion.
Then, he spoke this mantra:
Tadyathā: hara hara ra svāhā. I now proclaim that evil Māra relies upon his own power and might.
Manifesting various forms and colors, they came forward to confront him.
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva halted his army and,
acting as their brother, spoke these words:
For a thousand koṭis of kalpas, in my quest for bodhi,
I have relinquished my own life, as well as my sons and daughters,
and even my wealth and treasures, without any sense of stinginess.
Having made great vows, one cultivates this diligence and difficult ascetic practices;
for the sake of sentient beings, one initiates altruistic conduct,
aspiring to bring it to perfection through loving-kindness and compassion.
When that evil Māra saw this,
he came to create obstacles for me;
at that time, the Bodhisattva recollected this invincible Mahāvidyārājñī Dhāraṇī.
By the power of that illumination, Māra and his great host were all made to retreat and disperse.
Then he spoke this mantra:
*Tadyathā*: *iti mi ti* (1), *tira mitira* (2), *miti mile ni* (3), *svāhā* (4). Thereupon, the Vidyārāja manifested in the form of a woman.
Coming before the Bodhisattva, they joined their palms above their heads and spoke these verses:
"The Great Wisdom is proclaimed, Like a great light shining everywhere."
And today I have likewise subdued the armies of Māra;
just as you sought unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in the past and thereby attained great fearlessness,
so too have the armies of Māra been subdued.
Now, by the power of that illumination,
I shall destroy Māra, his great armies, and all his retinues.
Then he spoke this mantra:
*Tadyathā:* 1. *kāvaṭi*, 2. *kāvaṭa*, 3. *mule*, 4. *nākulā*, 5. *kukharā*, 6. *male ni*, 7. *svāhā*. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who causes all the world to attain the unsurpassed fruit— poison cannot harm him,
weapons cannot wound him, and fire cannot burn him.
Even during sleep, one will never see evil dreams;
nor shall one be bound by kings, nor fall into the hands of bandits,
nor encounter perilous mountain precipices, nor even [the dangers of] rivers and streams.
From all terrors and hardships, one attains complete liberation;
from all sins and afflictions, one is freed and becomes secure.
Through the power of clarity and the power of wisdom, one possesses great majesty and virtue.
Whatever task one undertakes, it shall be swiftly accomplished.
Then he spoke this mantra:
*Tadyathā: sūre, susūre, vara, vavara, manapava, samara, hūre, svāhā; mare, svāhā.* The Buddha said: "In the past, when I was seeking awakening..."
When I was a six-tusked white elephant,
I acted as a protector for that hunter;
if this is true, may all sentient beings [attain peace].
All sufferings and afflictions shall be completely eliminated.
In a past life, when I was a turtle in the ocean,
my body was subjected to cutting and slicing, yet my mind harbored no resentment.
If this is true, may all illnesses of all sentient beings be completely eradicated.
Then he spoke the mantra:
*Tadyathā:* *hile mile nirdūru vaṃ paṇe svāhā.* The Buddha said: "In the past, when I was seeking awakening (*bodhi*),..."
I bestow various forms of peace and happiness upon sentient beings.
In the past, when I was a pheasant captured by a hunter, I gave him what he required;
I cultivated the contemplation of loving-kindness and did not give rise to anger or resentment.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:
*Tadyathā | niri dudu duni mahānate svāhā | dudu duni hi ci mi ci ni ciri svāhā*. The Buddha said, "When I was a rishi practicing patience..."
Cultivating the contemplation of the perfection of patience,
the mind is free from affliction;
one observes all sentient beings as if they were one's own infants.
Blood flowed from my body and was transformed into milk.
When I was practicing universal giving in my quest for bodhi,
that brahmin came before me.
When they begged for my head and I gave it to them, they bound it to a tree with a rope of hair;
at that time, I gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, and felt no anger or resentment.
I regard the brahmins as if they were infants;
even my wife and concubines I give away entirely. I do not seek the pleasures of the five desires, nor the sovereignty of a king, nor the wealth and nobility of the heavens.
Truly, for the sake of subduing Māra and his retinue,
and even for taming all enemies to attain the supreme state,
one should utter the great mantra of great power in order to destroy them.
And being able to give rise to past practices and the conduct of awakening, in order to subdue Māra, I shall now further speak;
that is to say, I shall recite the mantra: *tadyathā | kiṃkiṇi | vimanaṇi | vi...*

"Oṃ, trayaścatvāriṃśat-prahaṇa-nanda-śubha-maye siddhi-siddhe saṃkhyā-vyayā-viśruta-te, I shall speak for you."
By the power, majesty, and diligence of that great mantra,
when the celestial hosts and the asuras were arrayed in opposing armies,
the devas recalled this [mantra], whereby they could not be defeated and the asuras themselves were subdued.
O Deva, with your diligence you shall contend against all the asuras;
for a thousand years of your celestial lifespan,
they shall watch for an opportunity, yet they shall be unable to gain the advantage.
If one lacks the power of true supremacy,
even if one achieves rebirth in the Brahma Heaven and constantly performs various activities, one will still be unable to surpass the majestic virtue of that Brahma.
And because it is for the purpose of making offerings, it was spoken by all the Buddhas.
He then spoke the mantra, saying:
*viśali* (1) *vibhūli* (2) *ṭikṣiṇi* (3) *suti*.
Cchindaya chindaya | agni-samīśe | amoghe apratihate | me kṣāpaya samatvaṃ kuru | mahāprabhaviṣṇo || 1 ||

The Buddha said: "During the latter part of the night, at the time when the sun first rises..."
To bring about the most supreme perfection of practice in the world,
to accomplish the deeds of a Buddha and attain enlightenment,
to subdue the armies of Māra, and to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, a multitude of a thousand koṭis of Śuddhāvāsa devas came before me and, with profound intent,
requested with gentle voices that the wheel of Dharma be turned.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Listen attentively, Śāriputra!
This Unconquerable King of Vidyās brings benefit, welfare, and peace to all sentient beings."
Śāriputra, in a past age,
the devas and the asuras engaged in battle with one another;
at that time, the hosts of devas retreated and dispersed, while the asuras achieved victory.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas,
immediately inscribed this Aparājita Dhāraṇī upon golden leaves and affixed them to the top of a banner.
They fought again,
and at that time the celestial hosts were victorious;
the army of the asuras immediately retreated and dispersed.
Then he spoke the mantra, saying:
*tadyathā | moṣe | vāsukare | nāgaranirje | kapaline | svāhā*. The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
I do not see any among the devas or Māras,
nor even among the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the human world,
including the asuras, all ghosts, or malevolent spirits.
Asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras,
mahoragas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas.
Even those such as the Kacchapūtana who consume raw flesh are unable to overcome this Great Vidyārāja, and none dare to transgress against it.
Such is the dhāraṇī of the Great Vidyārāja.
If one neither sees nor hears [it],
it is because of obstructions caused by past and present karma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having spoken this dhāraṇī for the accomplishment of all things, [concluded].
At that time, Ānanda, Śāriputra, devas, humans, asuras, and others,
received and upheld it with a single mind, rejoicing and practicing it accordingly.
Thus ends the *Buddhabhāṣita-anabhibhūta-mahāvidyārājñī-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
